title: Rates, Work & Speed
weightage: High — rate and work word problems appear on nearly every GRE, and the same logic drives Data Interpretation
intro: Almost every "rate" question on the GRE — miles per hour, jobs per day, dollars per pound, litres per minute — is the same relationship in different clothing: rate × time = amount. Get comfortable rearranging that one equation and the whole chapter opens up. The two ideas that trip people up are averages and teamwork. An average speed is never the plain average of two speeds when the times differ — it is total distance over total time, which is why a there-and-back trip at 40 and 60 does not average 50. And when two people or machines work together, you add their rates, not their times. The GRE keeps the numbers clean because the on-screen calculator is basic and slow, so the winning move is almost always to set up the right relationship and reason, not to grind. This chapter covers unit rates and conversions, the average-rate trap, the speed–distance–time triangle, and combined work — each with the fast method and the traps that quietly cost points.

items.name: Average speed
items.formula: total distance / total time (NOT the average of the speeds)

topics.name: Unit Rates & Unit Conversion
topics.details: A unit rate expresses "how much per one" — 45 miles per hour, $2.40 per pound, 12 pages per minute — and you get it by dividing the amount by the number of units. Unit rates make comparisons fair: to decide which package is the better buy, reduce each to a price per ounce and compare. Unit conversion is the same skill run in reverse: multiply by a conversion factor written as a fraction equal to 1, arranged so the unwanted unit cancels. To turn 90 km/h into metres per second, multiply by 1000 m / 1 km and by 1 h / 3600 s, and the km and h cancel to leave 25 m/s. The GRE mixes units on purpose — a speed in km/h with a time in minutes — so the reliable habit is to convert everything to consistent units before you compute. Because the calculator is basic, keep the conversion factors as simple fractions and cancel before multiplying.

solved.problem: A printer produces 320 pages in 8 minutes. Find its rate in pages per minute.
Which is cheaper per litre: 3 L for $8.40 or 5 L for $13.50?
solved.solution: 8.40/3 = $2.80 per L; 13.50/5 = $2.70 per L. The 5-litre pack is cheaper.

solved.problem: Convert 72 km/h into metres per second.
A car uses 6 litres of fuel per 100 km. How many litres for a 250 km trip?
solved.solution: Rate = 6 L per 100 km = 0.06 L/km. For 250 km: 250 × 0.06 = 15 litres.

unsolved.problem: A machine fills 450 bottles in 15 minutes. Find the rate in bottles per minute.
Which is the better value: 4 kg for $11.60 or 6 kg for $16.80?
hints: Find price per kg for each.

unsolved.problem: Convert 15 m/s to km/h.
A tap delivers 18 litres per minute. How many litres in 40 seconds?
hints: Convert the rate to per second.

unsolved.problem: A worker earns $153 for a 9-hour shift. What is the hourly rate, and the pay for 5 hours?

topics.name: Average Rate
topics.details: The single most tested trap in this chapter: average speed is total distance divided by total time, never the plain average of the individual speeds — unless the times spent are equal. If you drive 120 miles at 40 mph and the same 120 miles back at 60 mph, you spend 3 hours out and 2 hours back, so the average is 240 miles / 5 hours = 48 mph, not 50. When the two distances are equal, there is a clean shortcut: the average is the harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b) of the two speeds. When instead the two times are equal, the plain average does work. The GRE loves to reward the test-taker who spots which case they are in. The same logic covers average price when you buy different quantities, or average production rate across shifts — always rebuild it as total amount over total time or total units.

solved.problem: A cyclist rides 30 km at 15 km/h, then 30 km at 10 km/h. Find the average speed.
solved.solution: Time = 30/15 + 30/10 = 2 + 3 = 5 h for 60 km. Average = 60/5 = 12 km/h. (Harmonic mean: 2·15·10/25 = 12.)

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. A trip covers equal distances at 40 mph and 60 mph. Quantity A: the average speed. Quantity B: 50 mph. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Equal distances ⇒ average = 2·40·60/100 = 48 mph. So Quantity B (50) is greater. The plain-average 50 is the trap.

solved.problem: A driver travels for 2 hours at 50 km/h and 3 hours at 80 km/h. Find the average speed.
solved.solution: Distance = 100 + 240 = 340 km over 5 h. Average = 340/5 = 68 km/h.

solved.problem: A shopper buys 2 kg of apples at $3/kg and 3 kg at $4/kg. Find the average price per kg.
solved.solution: Total cost = 6 + 12 = $18 for 5 kg. Average = 18/5 = $3.60 per kg.

unsolved.problem: A car goes 60 km at 30 km/h and 60 km at 20 km/h. Find the average speed.
Equal distances are covered at 20 mph and 30 mph. Find the average speed.
A runner jogs 1 hour at 8 km/h and 2 hours at 5 km/h. Average speed?
A trip is half distance at 40 km/h and half at 60 km/h. Average speed?
A factory makes 200 units in the first 4 hours and 360 units in the next 6 hours. Average rate per hour?

topics.name: Speed, Distance & Time
topics.details: Everything here comes from distance = speed × time, rearranged as needed. Keep units consistent — a speed in km/h needs a time in hours, so convert 45 minutes to 0.75 h before multiplying. Two GRE staples deserve special attention. Relative speed: two objects moving toward each other close the gap at the sum of their speeds, while one chasing another closes it at the difference. So two trains approaching at 50 and 70 km/h close 120 km each hour; a car at 80 overtaking one at 60 gains 20 km/h. The other staple is the "same time" setup, where two travellers meet — set their distances to add up to the total, or set them equal for a catch-up. Because the calculator is basic, the GRE keeps these numbers friendly; your job is to translate the words into the right sum or difference of speeds.

solved.problem: A train travels at 72 km/h for 45 minutes. How far does it go?
solved.solution: Convert time: 45 min = 0.75 h. Distance = 72 × 0.75 = 54 km.

solved.problem: Two cyclists start 90 km apart and ride toward each other at 12 and 18 km/h. When do they meet?
A car leaves at 60 km/h. Two hours later a second car chases it at 80 km/h. How long until the second catches the first?
solved.solution: Head start = 60 × 2 = 120 km. Gain = 80 − 60 = 20 km/h. Catch-up time = 120/20 = 6 hours.

solved.problem: A 180 m train passes a stationary pole in 9 seconds. Find its speed in km/h.

unsolved.problem: A bus covers 210 km in 3.5 hours. Find its average speed.
How long does a 150 km trip take at 40 km/h? Give the answer in hours and minutes.
Two trains 300 km apart move toward each other at 40 and 60 km/h. When do they meet?
A runner at 10 km/h chases another 5 km ahead moving at 8 km/h. Catch-up time?
A 250 m train crosses a 150 m bridge in 20 seconds. Find its speed in m/s.

topics.name: Combined Work
topics.details: The golden rule of work problems: add rates, not times. If Ann paints a room in 4 hours, her rate is 1/4 of the room per hour; if Ben takes 6 hours, his rate is 1/6. Together they paint 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 of the room each hour, so the whole room takes 12/5 = 2.4 hours. For exactly two workers the shortcut is T = ab/(a + b) — the "product over sum" of the individual times. This idea covers pipes filling a tank (add fill rates), a drain working against a tap (subtract the drain’s rate), and staggered starts (one works alone for a while, then the other joins). The common wrong move is to average the times, which is meaningless — a fast helper should make the job take less time than either person alone, and only the rate method guarantees that. Keep the rates as clean fractions; the numbers are chosen so they combine neatly without the calculator.

solved.problem: Pipe A fills a tank in 4 hours, pipe B in 6 hours. How long together?
solved.solution: Combined rate = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 tank/hour. Time = 12/5 = 2.4 hours (2 h 24 min).

solved.problem: A can do a job in 10 days, B in 15 days. Working together, how many days?
A tank is filled by a tap in 3 hours but drained by a leak in 6 hours. With both open, how long to fill?
solved.solution: Net rate = 1/3 − 1/6 = 1/6 tank/hour, so it fills in 6 hours.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. A finishes a task in 8 hours, B in 8 hours. Quantity A: time for A and B working together. Quantity B: 4 hours. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Combined rate = 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4, so together they take exactly 4 hours. The quantities are equal.

unsolved.problem: X paints a fence in 12 hours, Y in 6 hours. How long together?
Two pipes fill a pool in 20 and 30 minutes respectively. How long together?
A does a job in 9 days, B in 18 days. Together, how many days?
A tap fills a tank in 5 hours; a drain empties it in 10 hours. Both open — fill time?
A and B together finish in 4 hours; A alone takes 6 hours. How long for B alone?

shortcuts: Everything is rate × time = amount. Write down which two you know and solve for the third — do not memorise separate formulas.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. The plain average of two speeds is right only when the times are equal.
Equal distances at speeds a and b ⇒ average speed = 2ab/(a + b) (the harmonic mean), always less than the plain average.
km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s, and m/s × 3.6 = km/h. Memorise this one conversion; it appears constantly.
Work problems: add rates, not times. Two workers of times a and b together take ab/(a + b).
Toward each other ⇒ add speeds; chasing ⇒ subtract speeds. Then time = gap ÷ relative speed.
mistakes: Averaging two speeds when the distances (not the times) are equal — you must use total distance over total time.
Mixing units: multiplying a km/h speed by a time left in minutes. Convert first.
Averaging times in a work problem instead of adding rates (a helper must reduce the time below either worker’s).
Forgetting to subtract a drain’s or headwind’s rate that works against the main rate.
In relative-speed problems, adding when you should subtract (catch-up) or vice versa (approach).
Adding the train length to nothing when it crosses a bridge — distance is train length PLUS bridge length.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — a round trip covers equal distances at 30 and 60 km/h. Quantity A: average speed. Quantity B: 45 km/h. Which is greater?
pyq.a: Quantity B. Equal distances ⇒ average = 2·30·60/90 = 40 km/h < 45. The tempting "45" is the plain-average trap.

pyq.q: Work — machine P does a job in 6 hours, machine Q in 3 hours. How long together?
Numeric Entry — a car travels 165 km in 2 hours 45 minutes. Enter its average speed in km/h.
Relative speed — two runners on a 400 m track start together and run in opposite directions at 5 and 3 m/s. When do they first meet?

summary: Every rate question is rate × time = amount in disguise, so identify the two quantities you know and solve for the third. Average speed is total distance over total time — the plain average of two speeds is a trap unless the times are equal, and for equal distances the answer is the harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b). In work problems, add rates rather than times: two workers of times a and b together take ab/(a + b), and a drain or headwind subtracts its rate. For moving objects, add speeds when they approach and subtract when one chases the other. Keep units consistent, remember km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s, and the GRE’s deliberately clean numbers fall out without leaning on the basic calculator.
